findings.description: Membership in CLOSURE_IDS does not guarantee that a blocker will actually close. A blocker can subsequently fail or be skipped because it depends on a bead the sweep keeps open.
findings.failure_mode: If A depends on B and B depends on kept bead C, processing A first force-closes A because B is a proposed closure. B then remains open because of C. The sweep has bypassed the dependency guard and closed A with an unresolved prerequisite.
findings.suggested_fix: Process closures in dependency order and retry blocked rows after successful closures. Only force-close a dependency cycle after verifying that the entire component can close without unresolved external blockers.
findings.failure_scenario: If A depends on B and B depends on kept bead C, processing A first force-closes A because B is a proposed closure. B then remains open because of C. The sweep has bypassed the dependency guard and closed A with an unresolved prerequisite.

findings.description: The sample parser runs inside process substitution, whose exit status is not checked. A malformed or truncated SAMPLE can therefore make jq fail without making --check fail.
findings.failure_mode: When SAMPLE contains invalid JSON before any complete row, the loop executes zero times, bad remains zero, and the script reports that all sampled closures were confirmed and exits successfully. This bypasses the re-verification gate on a corrupt artifact.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate and materialize the complete sample before entering the loop, checking jq's exit status explicitly. Reject an empty sample and malformed sample rows.
findings.failure_scenario: When SAMPLE contains invalid JSON before any complete row, the loop executes zero times, bad remains zero, and the script reports that all sampled closures were confirmed and exits successfully. This bypasses the re-verification gate on a corrupt artifact.

findings.description: An empty or comment-only exclusion file causes grep -v to exit 1. With pipefail, the EXJ assignment fails, and set -e terminates the script.
findings.failure_mode: A valid invocation with no excluded beads, represented by an empty file or a file containing only the documented ignored comments, exits before freezing any inventory.
findings.suggested_fix: Use awk alone to filter blank/comment lines and extract IDs, or explicitly handle grep's no-match exit status while preserving genuine read failures.
findings.failure_scenario: A valid invocation with no excluded beads, represented by an empty file or a file containing only the documented ignored comments, exits before freezing any inventory.

findings.description: `split -l "$BATCH" -d -a 2 --additional-suffix=.jsonl` uses GNU-coreutils-only options. `--additional-suffix` does not exist in BSD/macOS `split` or busybox `split` (and `-d` is absent on older macOS). The script sources `compat-lib.sh` three lines earlier specifically for `sha256_portable`, so non-GNU hosts are an explicit target of this codebase. Separately, `-a 2` fixes the suffix width at two digits, so any inventory that yields more than 100 batches (e.g. the live 329-bead inventory with `--batch-size` 1, 2 or 3, all of which pass the 1…100 argument check) makes GNU split fail with `output file suffixes exhausted`.
findings.failure_mode: On macOS/busybox the script aborts with `split: illegal option` AFTER `inventory.jsonl` and `inventory.sha256` have been written (lines 63 and 67) but before `batches/` and `INVENTORY.md` exist. The sweep directory is left half-frozen; the next invocation is refused as "frozen" and `--force` reproduces the same failure, so the tool is unusable on that host. The same partial-write ordering applies when `-a 2` runs out of suffixes on Linux.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `split` with a portable splitter (e.g. a short `awk 'NR%B==1{f=sprintf("%s/batch-%02d.jsonl", dir, int((NR-1)/B))} {print > f}'`, or a jq/bash loop), computing the suffix width from `ceil(N/BATCH)`. Also write to a temp dir and move into place only after every artifact is produced, so a failure never leaves a frozen-but-incomplete sweep directory.
findings.failure_scenario: On macOS/busybox the script aborts with `split: illegal option` AFTER `inventory.jsonl` and `inventory.sha256` have been written (lines 63 and 67) but before `batches/` and `INVENTORY.md` exist. The sweep directory is left half-frozen; the next invocation is refused as "frozen" and `--force` reproduces the same failure, so the tool is unusable on that host. The same partial-write ordering applies when `-a 2` runs out of suffixes on Linux.

findings.description: The idempotency claim ("a re-run skips applied ids") only holds when every closed bead has a line in `applied.jsonl`. The log line is written at lines 194-195 AFTER the `br close` mutation, so a bead becomes closed-but-unlogged if the script is interrupted between the two, if `br close` commits and then exits non-zero (e.g. a post-write JSONL sync failure, which `close_bead` turns into `failed` and does not log), or simply if a teammate closes the bead during the multi-day freeze→Explore→sample→apply window. In all three cases the validation at line 139-140 flags the bead as "not open in the tracker now" and the WHOLE re-run exits INVALID with nothing applied. The remedy text is wrong: "drop the row" trips the partition check (`inventory ids no manifest names`), and "demote to kept" puts a `backlog-2026-10` label and a "status: kept" comment on a bead that is actually closed. Note also that `DONE_IDS` is built with `jq ... || true`, so a corrupt `applied.jsonl` silently yields a partial id list and the same lockout.
findings.failure_mode: A single bead closed outside the sweep (or one crash mid-run) blocks every remaining row from being applied until the operator hand-appends a forged log line; following the printed remedy instead writes wrong label/comment data into the tracker.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat a closure row whose bead is already closed as satisfied: log it with `action: already-closed` and skip the `br close`, instead of failing validation. Alternatively write a `pending` log line before the mutation and finalize it after. Fail loudly (not `|| true`) when `applied.jsonl` does not parse, and fix the remedy text so it does not suggest dropping a row from a required partition.
findings.failure_scenario: A single bead closed outside the sweep (or one crash mid-run) blocks every remaining row from being applied until the operator hand-appends a forged log line; following the printed remedy instead writes wrong label/comment data into the tracker.

findings.description: `--force` is granted when every parsed blocker is in `CLOSURE_IDS`, i.e. on manifest INTENT, not on outcome. Rows are processed in manifest order, so bead A (blocked by B) can be force-closed before B is processed, and B may then come back `skipped-blocked` (its own blocker is `kept`), fail on a br error, or already be in the applied log as `skipped-blocked` from a previous run (SW-10 shows skipped-blocked rows are logged and skipped forever). The result is exactly the state br's dependency guard exists to prevent: A closed while its open blocker B stays open, and no re-run revisits A. Additionally the applied-log line for a forced close records `action: close` and the original `reason`, not the forced reason or a `forced: true` flag, so the audit trail the header promises ("reversible … citing this log") cannot distinguish forced closes.
findings.failure_mode: Dependency chains among the 174 closures (closure→closure→kept) silently produce closed beads whose blockers remain open; the only signal is the unrelated `skipped-blocked` line for B.
findings.suggested_fix: Do forced closes in a second pass after the first pass finishes, and only force when every blocker's row in THIS run ended with `ok=0` (actually closed), not merely when its manifest category starts with `closed`. Record `forced: true` and the blocker list in the applied-log line.
findings.failure_scenario: Dependency chains among the 174 closures (closure→closure→kept) silently produce closed beads whose blockers remain open; the only signal is the unrelated `skipped-blocked` line for B.

findings.description: The blocker list is recovered from br's stderr with `grep -oE 'blocked by: *[A-Za-z0-9, -]+' | head -1`. Two shapes of real output make the parsed list a strict SUBSET of the real blockers while still looking valid: (a) one `blocked by:` line per blocker, or a list wrapped onto a second line, where `head -1` keeps only the first; (b) any blocker id containing a character outside `[A-Za-z0-9, -]` (e.g. a hierarchical `bd-abc.1`), where the match stops at that character and everything after it is dropped. A subset that happens to consist only of this sweep's closures is then force-closed although an unparsed blocker is `kept`. The guard `[[ -n "$blockers" ]]` also passes on whitespace-only content (e.g. `blocked by: ,`), in which case the `for` loop iterates zero times and the function proceeds straight to `--force`. The regex is validated only against the test stub's single-line format; the one live `skipped-blocked` proves a match occurred, not that the list was complete.
findings.failure_mode: An unintended `--force` close of a bead whose real blocker is kept open, decided on a truncated blocker list.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not parse free-text stderr for a destructive decision. Query the tracker (`br show <id> --json` / dependency listing) for the open blockers and compare that structured list to `CLOSURE_IDS`. If you must parse, consider all `grep -o` matches (drop `head -1`), count words rather than testing `-n`, and refuse to force when the matched text is followed by anything other than end-of-line.
findings.failure_scenario: An unintended `--force` close of a bead whose real blocker is kept open, decided on a truncated blocker list.

findings.description: `EXJ="$(grep -v -E '^\s*(#|$)' "$EXCLUDE" | awk ... | jq ...)"` runs under `set -euo pipefail`. When the exclude file contains only comments and blank lines (or is empty), `grep -v` selects no lines and exits 1; pipefail propagates that as the substitution status, the assignment fails, and errexit terminates the script with exit 1 and no message, before `br list` runs. The header documents exit 1 as "br/jq failure".
findings.failure_mode: A cycle with no Tier 1 beads that passes a template exclude file (`# tier 1 ids` only) gets a silent exit 1 and no inventory; the operator is pointed at br/jq by the exit-code contract.
findings.suggested_fix: Append `|| true` to the grep stage (or use `{ grep ... || :; }`), and emit an explicit message when the exclude list resolves to zero ids.
findings.failure_scenario: A cycle with no Tier 1 beads that passes a template exclude file (`# tier 1 ids` only) gets a silent exit 1 and no inventory; the operator is pointed at br/jq by the exit-code contract.

findings.description: `br list --json --limit 5000` is used both to build the frozen inventory and, in `sweep-apply.sh` line 135, to decide which beads are still open. The jq filter afterwards drops `status == "closed"`, which implies the list may include closed beads, so the 5000 cap applies to the whole tracker, not to the open set. If the cap is hit, the inventory is silently incomplete (beads beyond the cut are never swept, with no warning), and in apply, open beads beyond the cut are reported as "not open in the tracker now (closed meanwhile?)", which is wrong. The same misreport happens when `br` itself fails in validate mode, because `2>/dev/null ... || true` turns a tracker error into an empty open set.
findings.failure_mode: Silent omission of beads from a sweep that claims to cover every open bead, and misleading validation failures that blame the manifests when the tracker call was truncated or failed.
findings.suggested_fix: Assert that the returned count is strictly below the limit (or page / use an unlimited flag) and fail with a clear message otherwise. In `sweep-apply.sh`, distinguish `br list` failure from an empty result and abort validation with a tracker error instead of per-row "closed meanwhile" messages.
findings.failure_scenario: Silent omission of beads from a sweep that claims to cover every open bead, and misleading validation failures that blame the manifests when the tracker call was truncated or failed.

findings.description: Answering concern 1 directly: the regex anchors and `[[ =~ ]]` are sound, `tr ';,'` cannot smuggle a resolving token, path refs cannot start with `-` in a harmful position because they are prefixed with `HEAD:`, and manifest ids are constrained to `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9-]*-[a-z0-9]+$` so they cannot escape `grep -qx`. No crafted bypass of a non-existent reference was found. However the path branch accepts ANY path at HEAD, including directories (`src/`, `.claude`) and repository-wide files (`README.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, which the tests themselves use as closure evidence). The evidence gate therefore checks that a reference exists, not that it relates to the bead; an Explore batch that writes `CHANGELOG.md` for every closure passes validation for all 174 closures.
findings.failure_mode: Closures with no real evidence pass validation as long as the evidence names any file in the tree; the 10% re-verification sample is the only remaining control.
findings.suggested_fix: At minimum reject directory paths (`git cat-file -t` must be `blob`) and a small denylist of repo-wide files (README, CHANGELOG, LICENSE), or require that path evidence also carry a commit/PR reference. Consider recording in the applied log which evidence token actually resolved.
findings.failure_scenario: Closures with no real evidence pass validation as long as the evidence names any file in the tree; the 10% re-verification sample is the only remaining control.
